Federal republic (pop., 2025: 47.6 million) in the far south of South America. The capital and largest city is [[Buenos Aires]], an autonomous city; the rest of the country is divided into 23 provinces. Argentina covers 2,780,085 sq km, making it the second-largest country in South America after Brazil, and borders Chile, Bolivia, Paraguay, Brazil, and Uruguay, with the South Atlantic Ocean to the east and the Drake Passage to the south. Its landscape ranges from the [[Andes]] to [[Patagonia]]. It claims sovereignty over the [[Falkland Islands]], South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, and part of Antarctica.

Human presence dates to the Paleolithic, and the [[Inca Empire]] expanded into the northwest in pre-Columbian times. Spanish colonization began in the 16th century, and Argentina succeeded the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata, founded in 1776. Independence was declared on July 9, 1816. Civil war lasted until 1880 and ended in reorganization as a federation, after which millions of European immigrants, mainly Italians and Spaniards, shaped its culture and demography. Coups occurred in 1930, 1943, 1955, 1962, 1966, and 1976, the last after the 1974 death of President [[Juan Perón]]. The military junta that followed killed thousands of critics in the Dirty War, which ended with the election of Raúl Alfonsín in 1983.

Argentina is a founding member of the UN and the World Trade Organization and belongs to the G20. Its economy is the second-largest in South America, and it ranks second in Latin America, after Chile, on the Human Development Index. Soybeans, corn, wheat, and beef are major exports, and the country has defaulted on its sovereign debt nine times since independence. Since [[Javier Milei]] became president in 2023, austerity and deregulation have accompanied a fall in annual inflation from nearly 300% to 36.6%, alongside recession and elevated poverty. Argentine culture is known internationally for [[Tango|tango]] and for writers such as Jorge Luis Borges.

Ancient Greek philosopher and polymath whose writings span the natural sciences, philosophy, linguistics, economics, politics, psychology, and the arts.

He was born in Stagira, in Chalkidiki in northern Greece, the son of Nicomachus, physician to King Amyntas of Macedon. Both parents died while he was young, and Proxenus of Atarneus became his guardian. At about 17 or 18 he moved to [[Athens]] to study at [[Plato]]'s Academy, where he remained for nearly 20 years, until Plato's death. He then settled for a time at Assos in Asia Minor, where he and Theophrastus researched botany and marine biology, continuing on [[Lesbos]]. In 343/42 BC [[Philip II of Macedon]] invited him to Pella to tutor his 13-year-old son, [[Alexander the Great]]. Returning to Athens in 335 BC, he founded the Lyceum, a school whose name for its members, Peripatetic, is linked to his habit of lecturing while walking; he also established a library there.

Aristotle wrote many treatises and dialogues, but only about a third of his output survives. His work contains the earliest known systematic study of [[Logic|logic]], including the syllogism, which shaped the field into the 19th century. In biology he classified animals on the basis of dissection and field observation. In the *Nicomachean Ethics* he held that human flourishing, *eudaimonia*, arises from rational virtue practiced in community, and in politics he analyzed 158 constitutions and advocated a blend of democracy and oligarchy called polity. Some of his doctrines, such as spontaneous generation and geocentric cosmology, were later overturned.

His physical science dominated from late antiquity into the Renaissance and was not systematically replaced until the Enlightenment and the rise of classical mechanics. Medieval Muslim scholars called him “The First Teacher,” and medieval Christians such as [[Thomas Aquinas]] called him simply “The Philosopher.” His ethics has drawn renewed interest with the modern revival of virtue ethics.

Elementary branch of mathematics concerned with numbers and the operations performed on them.

Its core operations are addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division; in a wider sense it also includes exponentiation, extraction of roots, and taking logarithms. The word derives from the Latin *arithmetica*, from the Greek *arithmos*, “number,” and *arithmetike tekhne*, “the art of counting.” Definitions differ. A narrow view restricts arithmetic to the natural numbers, but the more common view extends it to integers, rational numbers, real numbers, and sometimes complex numbers. It is closely related to [[Number theory|number theory]], which studies the properties of integers such as divisibility, factorization, and primality and is traditionally known as higher arithmetic.

The main kinds of numbers are [[Natural number|natural numbers]], which start from 1 and are also called counting numbers; whole numbers, which include 0; [[Integer|integers]], which add the negative whole numbers; and [[Rational number|rational numbers]], which are ratios of two integers. Every rational number corresponds to a finite or a repeating decimal. [[Irrational number|Irrational numbers]], such as π, cannot be expressed as a ratio of two integers and have infinite decimal representations without repetition. Rational and irrational numbers together make up the [[Real number|real numbers]].

Numbers are written in [[Numeral system|numeral systems]], which are either positional or non-positional. All early systems were non-positional, meaning a digit's value does not depend on its position; the simplest is the unary system, which repeats one symbol. Decimal arithmetic, using the numerals 0 to 9, is the most common, while binary arithmetic, using 0 and 1, is used by most computers.

Arithmetic is at least thousands and possibly tens of thousands of years old. Egyptians and Sumerians invented numeral systems for practical problems in about 3000 BC. The sources give Babylonian base-60 methods from around 2000 BC and Egyptian methods in the Rhind Papyrus from around 1650 BC. From the 7th and 6th centuries BC the ancient Greeks studied numbers more abstractly and introduced rigorous mathematical proof. The ancient Indians developed the concept of zero and the decimal system, which Arab mathematicians refined and spread to the Western world in the medieval period. The first mechanical calculators appeared in the 17th century, modern number theory and axiomatic foundations of arithmetic developed in the 18th and 19th centuries, and electronic calculators and computers transformed the speed and accuracy of calculation in the 20th.

Arithmetic underlies [[Algebra|algebra]], calculus, and statistics, plays a similar role in physics and economics, and is among the earliest forms of mathematics that students encounter. Its cognitive and conceptual foundations are studied by psychology and philosophy.

Covering that protects a person, animal, or vehicle from physical injury or damage, especially from weapons or projectiles in combat. The British spelling is armour.

Personal armor protects soldiers and war animals, while vehicle armor is used on warships, armored fighting vehicles, and some combat aircraft, mostly ground attack aircraft. It is also worn against hazards in activities such as cycling and construction. The word also names armored forces: after the development of armored warfare, tanks and mechanized infantry came to be called collectively “armor.” The word comes from Old French *armure*, from Latin *armatura*, and is dated in English from 1297.

Armor has been used throughout recorded history, evolving from leather and fabric through chain mail and metal plate to modern composites. The first record of body armor appears on the Stele of Vultures in ancient [[Sumer]], and scale mail is attested in New Kingdom Egypt, Zhou dynasty China, and dynastic India. Cuirasses and helmets were made in Japan as early as the 4th century. Mail made of interlocking iron rings is believed to have first appeared some time after 300 BC; its invention is credited to the [[Celts]], and the Romans are thought to have adopted it. Roman legions also wore the *lorica squamata* and *lorica segmentata*. Plate armor became widespread in medieval Europe when water-powered trip hammers made the forming of plates faster and cheaper. Breast and back plates were worn by heavy cavalry in several European countries until the first year of [[World War I]] (1914–15).

The manufacture of armor drove technologies of the ancient world, including wood lamination, mining, metal refining, and leather processing, and influenced the [[Industrial Revolution]]. It was also an important factor in the development of [[Firearm|firearms]], which in turn revolutionized warfare and gradually made heavy plate obsolete on the battlefield. Modern body armor uses materials such as [[Kevlar]] and ceramics to stop bullets.

Diverse range of human activity centered on works made as expressions of creativity or imagination, expected to give an audience a worthwhile experience of emotion, thinking, or beauty.

There is no strictly agreed definition of art, and its interpretation has varied greatly across history and cultures. Some theorists think the typical concept of artistic works does not fit well outside modern Western societies. In the Western tradition, the three classical branches of visual art are [[Painting|painting]], [[Sculpture|sculpture]], and [[Architecture|architecture]]; theatre, dance, other performing arts, literature, music, and film are included in the broader “arts.” The word comes from a Latin sense meaning “skill” or “craft,” and until the 17th century art referred to any skill or mastery, without distinction from crafts or sciences. After the 17th century, where aesthetic considerations are paramount, the fine arts were separated from acquired skills in general, such as the decorative or applied arts. Some argue that the difference between fine and applied art reflects value judgments more than any clear definitional difference.

The purposes of art include communicating ideas, creating beauty, exploring the nature of perception, giving pleasure, and generating strong emotions. Philosophers including [[Plato]], [[Aristotle]], Socrates, and [[Immanuel Kant]] questioned its meaning. In the *Republic*, Plato’s Socrates wants to outlaw Homer’s poetry, while in the *Phaedrus* he says poetry is inspired by the Muses. Aristotle considered epic poetry, tragedy, comedy, dithyrambic poetry, and music to be imitative arts that differ in medium, object, and manner, and held that imitation is natural to humankind. Kant took science to represent the domain of knowledge and the arts the domain of the freedom of expression.

The nature of art and related concepts such as creativity and interpretation are explored in the branch of philosophy known as [[Aesthetics|aesthetics]], and artworks are studied in [[Art criticism|art criticism]] and art history. Evidence of symbolic marking dates to at least 73,000 years ago, in abstract markings on rocks in South Africa, and figurative depictions of animals and human-like figures appear around 51,200 years ago in caves in Sulawesi, Indonesia. AI-generated and AI-assisted work has intensified debates over authorship, creativity, and agency.

General term for disorders of the joints, marked by pain and stiffness.

Symptoms generally include joint pain and stiffness, and may include redness, warmth, swelling, and decreased range of motion. Onset can be gradual or sudden, and in some types other organs, such as the skin, are also affected. The term derives from *arthr-*, “joint,” and *-itis*, “inflammation.” Grouped under it are more than 100 conditions, including osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, gout, lupus, spondyloarthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and septic arthritis.

The most common form is [[Osteoarthritis]], which affects more than 3.8% of people. It usually occurs with age, often in the hips, knees, shoulders, and fingers, and results from damage to joint [[Cartilage|cartilage]] through prior injury or long-term wear. [[Rheumatoid arthritis]], the second most common at about 0.24%, is an autoimmune disorder that often affects the hands and feet, in which the [[Immune system|immune system]] attacks the lining of the joint capsule. [[Gout]] is caused by urate crystals depositing in joints after excessive uric acid production. [[Lupus]] can also affect the joints.

Risk factors include age, obesity, previous joint injury, and, for inflammatory types, female sex, family history, and exposure to tobacco smoke. Diagnosis rests on clinical examination, supported by imaging and blood tests. Rheumatoid arthritis is generally worse in the morning, with stiffness lasting over 30 minutes.

There is no cure for most types. Early treatment commonly includes resting the joint and applying heat or ice; weight loss and exercise may reduce force across weight-bearing joints. Medications such as [[Ibuprofen|ibuprofen]] and [[Paracetamol|acetaminophen]] relieve symptoms, disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs are used for autoimmune forms, and severe cases may require joint replacement surgery.

About 15% of people in Australia and more than 20% in the United States have a type of arthritis. It becomes more common with age and is a common reason people cannot work.

Invertebrate of the phylum Arthropoda, with a segmented body, paired jointed appendages, and an exoskeleton.

The exoskeleton, or cuticle, is made of [[Chitin|chitin]] and is often mineralized with calcium carbonate. To grow, arthropods must go through stages of [[Moulting|molting]], shedding the exoskeleton to reveal a new one. The name comes from the Greek *arthron*, “joint,” and *pous*, “foot,” and the designation Arthropoda was first used in 1843 by the German zoologist Johann Ludwig Christian Gravenhorst.

Arthropoda is the largest animal phylum, with estimates of species ranging from 1,170,000 to 5–10 million and accounting for over 80 percent of all known living animal species. A 1992 study estimated that of 500,000 species of animals and plants in Costa Rica alone, 365,000 were arthropods. They live in marine, freshwater, land, and air ecosystems. The phylum is divided into four major groups: [[Chelicerata]] (including arachnids and horseshoe crabs), [[Myriapoda]] (centipedes and millipedes), [[Crustacean|Crustacea]] (crabs, shrimp, lobsters, and other mostly aquatic forms), and [[Hexapoda]], which includes the [[Insect|insects]], the group with the most described species of any class. Both the smallest and the largest arthropods are crustaceans.

Hemolymph, the analogue of blood, circulates through an open circulatory system. The nervous system is ladder-like, with paired ventral nerve cords, and the brain, formed by fusion of ganglia, encircles the esophagus. Vision relies on compound eyes and simple ocelli, although the main eyes of spiders are ocelli that can form images. All terrestrial species use internal fertilization, and almost all arthropods lay eggs, though a few, such as aphids and scorpions, are genuinely viviparous. Hatchlings range from miniature adults to grubs and caterpillars that undergo total metamorphosis.

Arthropod ancestry dates to the [[Cambrian]] period. The group is generally regarded as monophyletic, though relationships among its subgroups are still debated. Arthropods contribute to the human food supply directly as food and, more importantly, as pollinators of crops, while some species spread severe disease to humans, livestock, and crops.

Capability of computational systems to perform tasks typically associated with human intelligence, such as learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, and decision-making; also the field of research that develops such systems.

As a field it spans [[Computer science|computer science]], engineering, and mathematics, and draws on psychology, linguistics, philosophy, and neuroscience. Its traditional goals include learning, reasoning, knowledge representation, planning, natural language processing, and perception, with support for robotics. Techniques include state space search, mathematical optimization, formal logic, [[Neural network (machine learning)|artificial neural networks]], and methods from statistics, operations research, and economics. Applications include web search engines, [[Chatbot|chatbots]], virtual assistants, autonomous vehicles, play and analysis in strategy games such as chess and Go, and content generation.

The term is credited to John McCarthy, in a 1955 proposal for the Dartmouth Conference held in 1956, and AI was founded as an academic discipline in 1956. The field went through cycles of optimism alternating with periods of disappointment and lost funding known as AI winters. Early researchers built algorithms imitating step-by-step reasoning; by the late 1980s and 1990s, methods for uncertain information using probability and economics had been developed. Interest and funding grew substantially after 2012, when [[Graphics processing unit|graphics processing units]] began to accelerate neural networks and [[Deep learning|deep learning]] outperformed earlier techniques. DeepMind’s AlphaGo mastered Go in 2016, and growth accelerated further after 2017 with the transformer architecture. Advances in [[Generative AI|generative AI]], which creates and modifies media, spurred the AI boom of the 2020s. Reasoning models, a type of [[Large language model|large language model]] trained to generate intermediate chains of thought, emerged in 2024 and improved performance on mathematics and coding, though they can still produce incorrect outputs known as hallucinations.

Some companies, including OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Meta, aim to create [[Artificial general intelligence]], AI able to complete nearly any cognitive task at least as well as a human; it has not been achieved. AI safety, unintended harms, ethical concerns, environmental effects, and potential existential risks have prompted discussions of AI regulation.

Emperor of [[Magadha]] and third ruler of the [[Maurya Empire]] (r. c. 268–232 BC), also spelled Asoka.

His empire covered much of the Indian subcontinent, stretching from present-day [[Afghanistan]] in the west to present-day [[Bangladesh]] in the east, with its capital at Pataliputra. According to his edicts, in his eighth regnal year (c. 260 BC) he conquered Kalinga after a brutal war; the edicts claim over 100,000 deaths and 150,000 deportations and express his remorse. He then devoted himself to the propagation of *dhamma*, or righteous conduct, a policy emphasizing non-violence, tolerance of sects, animal welfare, and public works.

The edicts, inscribed in Prakrit in Brahmi script on rocks and polished sandstone pillars, with versions in Greek and [[Aramaic]] in western provinces, are the earliest self-representations of imperial power in the Indian subcontinent. They suggest that a few years after the Kalinga War he was gradually drawn toward [[Buddhism]]. Buddhist legends credit him with establishing many stupas, patronizing the Third Buddhist council, supporting missionaries, including his son Mahinda to Sri Lanka, and making generous donations to the monastic community.

The sources have limits. The inscriptions focus mainly on dhamma, and the American scholar John S. Strong has suggested they are sometimes best read as propaganda aimed at presenting a favorable image of Ashoka and his administration. The legends were composed by Buddhist authors long after his reign and fall into two main traditions, a North Indian one and a Sri Lankan one, that differ on events such as the Third Buddhist council. Modern scholars range from dismissing them as mythological to accepting the plausible portions.

Ashoka’s existence as a historical emperor had almost been forgotten until the 19th-century decipherment of sources in Brahmi script. The State Emblem of the Republic of India is an adaptation of the Lion Capital of Ashoka, and the Ashoka Chakra, or Ashoka’s wheel, appears at the center of the [[Flag of India|national flag]].

Largest continent in the world by both land area and population, forming the eastern part of the landmass of [[Eurasia]].

Asia covers more than 44 million sq km, about 30% of Earth’s total land area and 8% of its total surface area. Its 4.7 billion people make up roughly 60% of the world’s population. It is bounded on the east by the Pacific Ocean, on the south by the Indian Ocean, and on the north by the Arctic Ocean. The boundary with Europe is a historical and cultural construct, since there is no clear physical separation. A commonly accepted division places Asia east of the Turkish straits, the [[Ural Mountains]] and Ural River, and south of the [[Caucasus Mountains]] and the Caspian and Black seas. The boundary with Africa follows the [[Suez Canal]], the Gulf of Suez, the Red Sea, and the Bab-el-Mandeb, which makes Egypt a transcontinental country with the Sinai Peninsula in Asia. The border with Oceania is usually placed in the Indonesian Archipelago, near the Wallace Line.

The concept of Asia derives from the term for the eastern region from a European perspective, and the boundary has moved since classical antiquity. Anaximander placed it along the Phasis River in Georgia, a convention Herodotus followed; in the Hellenistic period it was moved to the Tanais, the modern Don. In 1730 Philip Johan von Strahlenberg proposed the Ural Mountains, and the Ural River prevailed in the mid-19th century. The name is believed to originate in the Bronze Age toponym Assuwa, which referred to a portion of northwestern Anatolia and appears in Hittite records of a rebellion against King Tudhaliya I around 1400 BC. [[Herodotus]] used the term for Anatolia and the Achaemenid Empire, and the Roman writer Pliny was among the first to apply it to the whole continent.

Asia was the site of many of the first civilizations, including those of [[Mesopotamia]], the Indus Valley, and ancient China, and the birthplace of most mainstream religions, including Islam, Judaism, Christianity, Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism. China and India traded places as the largest economies in the world from 1 to 1800 CE. The [[Silk Road]] became the main east–west trading route in the Asian interior, and the Straits of Malacca a major sea route. Asia grew economically and in population during the 20th century, though overall population growth has since fallen.

The continent varies greatly in ethnic groups, cultures, economies, and governments. Its terrain includes the [[Himalayas]], whose Mount Everest rises 8,848.86 m, the Tibetan Plateau, and deserts such as the Gobi and Arabian, and its climates range from equatorial to subarctic and polar. It contains 48 sovereign countries.
